title: Postoperative bleeding
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise suspected postoperative haemorrhagic shock from combined physiological and wound/drain changes and escalate immediately.
Take first-line nursing actions (reinforce the dressing, mark the drainage, stay with the patient) and tell the surgeon how much has been lost.
Raise anticoagulant doses with the prescriber when bleeding is suspected.
Support fluids and blood products as ordered, and hand over clearly.
Report evolving platelet/coagulation abnormalities alongside blood loss and perfusion without claiming one clotting test establishes a DIC diagnosis or directs component choice.

setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit six hours after abdominal surgery, receiving an anticoagulant for clot prevention.

steps.info: During postoperative observations, the wound dressing contains more blood than at the previous check. The patient is pale, cold and clammy, with a faster pulse and falling pressure. The extent of blood loss is not yet known.
steps.prompt: Which immediate response addresses possible haemorrhagic shock without delaying assessment to quantify visible bleeding?

observations.label: Blood loss
observations.value: Wound and drain loss require quantification

options.text: Assess breathing and circulation at bedside; call the urgent clinical response for suspected haemorrhagic shock and alert the surgeon. Ask a colleague to quantify blood loss without delaying assessment.
options.feedback: Blood loss with reduced blood pressure, tachycardia and cool skin may indicate serious postoperative bleeding and shock. The urgent response and bedside assessment take priority over dressing documentation; communicate the wound, drain and physiological trend as the team arrives. The 2025 Association of Anaesthetists guidance emphasizes early recognition, coordinated blood-bank communication and definitive bleeding control. Suspected life-threatening haemorrhage warrants the local emergency pathway; do not wait for a particular haemoglobin or coagulation result before escalating.
options.consequence: Early assessment and surgical escalation may accelerate resuscitation and identification of ongoing bleeding.

options.text: Remove the dressing to inspect the wound, apply a clean dressing and record the appearance for later documentation without informing the surgeon or requesting urgent assessment of the patient's changing observations.
options.feedback: The first dressing is normally managed by the surgeon; the nurse reinforces it and reports excessive bleeding rather than hiding it under a clean dressing.
options.consequence: An unreported dressing change could obscure the trend in blood loss and delay recognition of deterioration.

options.text: Compare the wound and drain findings with previous readings, document the pressure change and wait for the surgeon's scheduled round before requesting a clinical assessment.
options.feedback: Excessive bleeding with changes in the vital signs should prompt medical evaluation at once.
options.consequence: Waiting for the ward round could allow further blood loss and worsening perfusion.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, the patient is increasingly anxious and pressure has fallen further. The surgical team has been alerted. IV access is working and a scheduled anticoagulant dose is due; the active bleeding concern has not resolved.
steps.prompt: How should the nurse address the due anticoagulant and prepare for urgent haemorrhage management?

options.text: Stay, assess haemodynamics and ask the prescriber to reassess the due anticoagulant before giving it. Coordinate ordered tests, products, fluids or theatre transfer.
options.feedback: Suspected postoperative haemorrhage needs urgent clinician review of anticoagulation as well as bleeding control and resuscitation. A due medication is not an instruction to ignore active deterioration; dose omission, reversal, component selection and resuscitation orders follow an authorised pathway. Coordinate activation of the local major-haemorrhage pathway and correctly identified samples with colleagues as directed; avoid delaying urgent clinical assessment while waiting for routine laboratory turnaround.
options.consequence: Prompt medication review and coordinated preparation may prevent additional bleeding risk without delaying urgent resuscitation.

options.text: Administer the scheduled anticoagulant because the prescription remains on the chart; document administration and report the bleeding to the surgeon afterwards.
options.feedback: An anticoagulant given to a patient who may be bleeding can worsen the haemorrhage; the prescriber must be asked first.
options.consequence: Giving anticoagulation before reassessment could aggravate bleeding.

options.text: Leave the bedside to collect anticipated blood products without first coordinating the team's orders or arranging continued observation.
options.feedback: Leaving an actively deteriorating patient unobserved to collect blood products is unsafe. Stay with the patient and coordinate the urgent team's authorised blood-product preparation through another staff member.
options.consequence: Leaving the bedside could interrupt surveillance during ongoing haemodynamic deterioration.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the team has prescribed fluids and blood products and is considering return to theatre. Pressure is responding slowly, urine output is falling, and repeat coagulation and platelet results are pending. Effective haemostasis has not been established.
steps.prompt: What must the nurse continue to verify, monitor and communicate during emergency resuscitation?

observations.label: Orders
observations.value: Fluids and blood products prescribed by the clinical team

options.text: Give ordered resuscitation using emergency transfusion identification and reaction-monitoring procedures. Reassess perfusion, urine and temperature; report loss, coagulation, ionized calcium and potassium without assigning a DIC diagnosis. Hand over.
options.feedback: Blood-product selection, emergency issue procedures, haemostatic treatments and return-to-theatre decisions belong to the responsible team. Rapid nursing reassessment and appropriately authorised transfusion safety checks continue while haemorrhage is treated; platelet, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer trends are context for the team and do not by themselves diagnose DIC. During major haemorrhage and transfusion, electrolyte abnormalities including hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia can require prompt clinician-directed treatment. Alongside bedside observations, trend ordered blood counts, clotting tests, acid–base status, ionized calcium and temperature during active major haemorrhage. Escalate worsening results and coordinate the approved warming and haemorrhage pathway; sampling intervals depend on the clinical situation and institutional protocol. Do not independently choose components or electrolyte replacement. Communicate whether bleeding is ongoing and whether resuscitation is effective. The responsible team coordinates definitive haemostasis and deactivates the major-haemorrhage pathway when appropriate, with the blood bank informed. During active major haemorrhage, new hypotension needs immediate senior assessment of ongoing blood loss versus a possible component reaction. Coordinate lifesaving resuscitation without waiting for laboratory results; the responsible team determines whether transfusion can continue or a different component is needed. Do not independently continue or restart a suspect component.
options.consequence: Coordinated transfusion safeguards and serial perfusion, blood loss and laboratory assessment may help the team identify ongoing haemorrhage or treatment complications.

options.text: Start the blood without completing the hospital's emergency identification and patient-monitoring safeguards, reasoning that the urgency of bleeding makes the checks unnecessary until transfer; document administration and notify the receiving team later.
options.feedback: Even during major haemorrhage, transfusion follows the hospital's emergency issue and patient-identification pathway, with appropriate safety and reaction monitoring; staff must use its specified emergency checks rather than inventing an exception.
options.consequence: Bypassing emergency identification safeguards could expose the patient to an incompatible component or delay recognition of a reaction.

options.text: Focus on delivering prescribed resuscitation and blood products, and suspend urine-output recording and serial observations until transfer is complete, leaving the receiving team to establish the response to treatment.
options.feedback: Fluid status and urine output are monitored closely in a patient who is bleeding.
options.consequence: Stopping observations could conceal persistent hypoperfusion despite ongoing resuscitation.

learning_points: Falling pressure, a fast pulse and cool skin with postoperative wound bleeding justify immediate patient-first assessment and urgent response; measuring and marking wound drainage must not delay getting clinical help.
Do not take the first dressing off and hide the evidence; the surgeon needs to see it.
Raise any due anticoagulant dose with the prescriber when bleeding is suspected.

Resuscitation, transfusion and possible return to theatre remain clinician-directed; use the authorised emergency blood-identification pathway, track perfusion/urine output and give timely blood-loss and laboratory-trend handover.

Falling platelets, abnormal clotting tests or a normal fibrinogen cannot independently determine DIC or blood-product selection; communicate clinical and laboratory trends while the team investigates.
Monitor temperature and ordered ionized calcium and potassium during major haemorrhage resuscitation; communicate abnormalities promptly and follow the authorised treatment pathway.
Escalate suspected life-threatening bleeding without waiting for a single laboratory threshold; coordinate communication with the clinical team and blood bank, and definitive haemorrhage control.

During active major haemorrhage, new hypotension needs immediate senior assessment of ongoing blood loss versus a possible component reaction. Coordinate lifesaving resuscitation without waiting for laboratory results; the responsible team determines whether transfusion can continue or a different component is needed. Do not independently continue or restart a suspect component.
